scenario.name: Mission 2: Ransomed Trust - Hospital Backup Server
scenario.author: Z. Cliffe Schreuders
scenario.description:
# Mission 2: Ransomed Trust
St. Catherine's Regional Medical Centre has been hit by ransomware. Patients on life support are at risk. ENTROPY has encrypted critical hospital systems and is demanding £150,000 in Bitcoin.
You have been deployed to investigate the attack and restore hospital operations. ENTROPY got in weeks ago, with help from someone inside, and exploited an unpatched ProFTPD backdoor on the hospital's backup server.
## Your Objectives
1. **Gain access to the hospital backup server** - The server is running a vulnerable ProFTPD service 2. **Locate Ghost's operational files** - Evidence of the infiltration is on the system 3. **Recover the offline backup keys** - These keys can decrypt patient data without paying the ransom 4. **Identify the insider** - Find the evidence that points to who helped ENTROPY in 5. **Trace ENTROPY's attack methodology** - Understand how they penetrated hospital security
## Investigation Brief
**IT Administrator**: Gary Whitlock warned hospital management about the ProFTPD vulnerability for months. His warnings were ignored. ENTROPY is now using him as a scapegoat.
**Network Bridge**: A wireless network bridge was planted in the IT department, giving ENTROPY a remote foothold on the backup server.
**Operational Files**: Ghost's files on the server should reveal the full scope of the infiltration and the evidence that leads to the insider.
**Database Backup**: The server contains encrypted patient database backups and the restore catalogue. Finding them opens the path to Ghost's operational logs and clears Gary Whitlock.
## Technical Challenge Path
You will need to: - Exploit the ProFTPD 1.3.3c distribution backdoor (OSVDB-69562; no CVE assigned) - Reach the restricted files - Decode Ghost's obfuscated operational files - Connect the technical evidence to the physical investigation (the cracker device in the sealed case, and the badge that held the doors)
## Narrative Payoff
Successfully rooting this server will: - Show that Gary Whitlock was warning about the vulnerability all along - Surface the evidence that identifies the insider - Point to the escrow safe the attackers staged against - Lay out ENTROPY's infiltration methodology end to end - Connect the VM challenge to the physical escape room investigation
Ghost doesn't know you're coming. Make it count.

From: Gary Whitlock (IT Systems) To: Dr. Sarah Kim (CTO) CC: Board Secretariat Date: 8 November Subject: URGENT -- ProFTPD 1.3.3c backdoor on backup server
Dr Kim,
Seventh time of asking. The backup server is still running ProFTPD 1.3.3c -- the trojaned source release from 2010. That build carries a backdoor in its own source code, which gives an attacker remote code execution with no credentials at all. A clean version has been available since 2010.
This box holds every clinical backup we have. If it goes, the wards go with it.
I have costed the remediation at £85,000. That is the whole ask. I am not asking for a project, I am asking for a server that is not fourteen years out of date.
Please put this in front of the board as CRITICAL and not as an IT wish-list item.
Gary

ST. CATHERINE'S HOSPITAL - BACKUP AND RECOVERY PROCEDURES
OFFLINE RECOVERY KEYS Location: Emergency escrow safe (physical security) Access: 4-digit PIN PIN: the hospital's founding year -- never changed, flagged at three audits Holder of record: IT Director
ONLINE RECOVERY KEYS Location: /var/backups/hospital_db/ Encryption: AES-256 Access: Root user only
RESTORE CATALOGUE Location: /var/backups/hospital_db/ Purpose: identifies the last clean snapshot. The recovery console will not restore anything without it -- it cannot tell a clean snapshot from a poisoned one.
RECOVERY PROCEDURE: 1. Retrieve the offline keys from the escrow safe 2. Combine with the online recovery keys from this server 3. Confirm the clean snapshot against the restore catalogue 4. Decrypt and restore patient databases to production
NOTE: both key sets and the catalogue are required for a full recovery. Gary Whitlock documented this procedure after management declined a proper off-site backup.
For investigation of suspected intrusion, check: /root/.ghost_ops/ directory (if it exists - indicates compromise)

OPERATION RANSOMED TRUST - EQUIPMENT DEPLOYMENT LOG ====================================================
INFILTRATION TIMELINE: Week 1: Network bridge deployment Week 3: Emergency storage reconnaissance Week 6: ProFTPD exploit execution
SITE SELECTION: -------------- St. Catherine's was not the weakest target of the 214 hospitals surveyed. It was the cleanest. Seven written warnings from one administrator (G. Whitlock, IT Systems), each one answered, each one deferred by the CTO. The paper trail is immaculate. When this becomes public there will be no argument about whether they knew. That is the whole point of the choice.
INSIDE CONTACT: -------------- Status: ACTIVE. Unpaid. The contact came to us -- a grievance of their own, not a wage. No money has changed hands and none will. Do not offer further payment. Access: an internal override badge. It ran the unscheduled fire drill six weeks ago, when the "fire safety" contractor sweep placed the bridge, and it held the doors again during Friday's drill.
EQUIPMENT ISSUED: ---------------- 1. Wireless Network Bridge (Netgear R6400) - Location: IT Department, hidden behind the server rack - Purpose: Remote access foothold - Status: Deployed Week 1, operational
2. PIN Cracker Device - Location: Server Room, inside the sealed case in the maintenance rack - Purpose: Staged against the emergency escrow safe (the PIN is the hospital's founding year, never changed) - Status: Concealed Week 6, ready for recovery
3. ProFTPD 1.3.3c Backdoor Exploit Payload - Deployment: Week 6 via network bridge - Execution: Successful - Ransom note delivered: Confirmed
RANSOM: ------ Amount: £150,000, payable in BTC at the prevailing rate Payment wallet: bc1q7cyrfmckn2ewz5m78ts6jt9lcfhfwcvzefm27k Settlement: Syndicate cut 30% / Operator cut 70%. Architect approval: CONFIRMED. Projected success at this site: 94% (upgrades deferred, systems unpatched).
OPERATIONAL SECURITY: -------------------- - The contact has a legitimate reason to be on the floor. Plausible deniability holds. - Equipment serials sanitized (untraceable to ENTROPY) - Payment routed through 3 BTC mixers - If the contact is compromised: DENY ALL KNOWLEDGE
-- Ghost, Ransomware Incorporated

ST. CATHERINE'S HOSPITAL - BACKUP SERVER =========================================
FTP Service: ProFTPD 1.3.3c Status: ACTIVE Anonymous Access: READ-ONLY
Available Backups: - /backups/public/system_configs/ (public) - /backups/public/application_logs/ (public)
RESTRICTED AREAS (requires authentication): - /var/backups/hospital_db/ (encrypted patient data) - /root/.ghost_ops/ (UNAUTHORIZED - investigate if found)
For authorized access, contact: Gary Whitlock (gwhitlock@stcatherines.hospital)
System Administrator: Gary Whitlock Last Security Audit: OVERDUE (6 months) Known Vulnerabilities: UNPATCHED (management decision)

OPERATION RANSOMED TRUST - GHOST'S OPERATIONAL LOG (ENCODED) ===================================
WINDOW CONFIRMATION: The entry window was held open during Friday's fire drill, 02:30-03:00. Internal override badge SC-4471 ran that drill and silenced the panel, as it ran the drill six weeks ago when the "fire safety" contractor sweep placed the bridge. That badge is what put us on the floor. The estate went dark at 02:47, inside the window.
ON THE INSIDE CONTACT: No name in this log, and none in the next. They came to us, not the other way round -- a grievance, not a wage. No money has changed hands. If anyone ever traces the badge, let them: SC-4471 leads to a post, not to a payroll.
KEY MATERIAL: Ghost's session keys and the restore-catalogue override are staged in the cache in the server-room rack, behind the sealed case. Recover them before the recovery console is touched.
STANDING ORDERS: - Eyes on the ground. Report any investigation. - Do not interfere with the ransom process. - Hold the line. Deny everything.
-- Ghost, Ransomware Incorporated
